title: Sets, Relations, and Functions
tagline: The vocabulary of mathematics: sets define collections, relations capture structure between elements, and functions are the maps that connect every computation.

sections.content:
Mathematics is a language, and like every language it has a vocabulary. **Sets, relations, and functions** are that vocabulary's most fundamental words. Before you can talk rigorously about graphs, databases, type systems, formal languages, algorithms, or probability, you need these three ideas — not just as definitions to memorise, but as flexible tools you reach for automatically when reasoning about structure.

A **set** is deceptively simple: an unordered collection of distinct objects called elements. That simplicity is the point. Because a set makes no commitment about order, repetition, or representation, it can model anything: {1, 2, 3}, the set of all prime numbers, the set of all valid SQL queries, even the empty set ∅ that contains nothing at all. Set operations — union (∪), intersection (∩), difference (\\), symmetric difference (△), complement, and Cartesian product (×) — let you construct, compare, and combine these collections, and they map directly onto SQL joins, type system unions and intersections, network packet filtering, and database schema design.

A **relation** on sets A and B is simply any subset of the Cartesian product A × B — a collection of ordered pairs. Relations are everywhere: 'x divides y', 'person x follows person y on Twitter', 'state x can transition to state y in a finite automaton', 'class x is a subtype of y in a type hierarchy'. The power of the relational model comes from classifying relations by their structural properties: reflexivity, symmetry, antisymmetry, transitivity. These properties carve out named families — equivalence relations, partial orders, total orders — each with a rich theory and concrete CS applications.

A **function** is a special kind of relation with one key constraint: every input maps to exactly one output. Functions are the heartbeat of computation. Every algorithm is a function from inputs to outputs. Every pure function in functional programming is literally a mathematical function. The classification of functions — **injective** (one-to-one, no two inputs share an output), **surjective** (onto, every output is reachable), and **bijective** (both) — underlies counting arguments, the theory of encryption and perfect hashing, type isomorphisms, and Cantor's revolutionary work on the sizes of infinite sets.

This chapter builds all three ideas from scratch, connects each to concrete code, and shows why they are not abstract formalities but practical thinking tools you will use in every domain of computer science.

sections.title: Sets as Guest Lists, Relations as Seating Charts, Functions as Hotel Room Keys
sections.content:
Picture organising a large conference. The **set** of registered attendees is a guest list — a collection where each name appears at most once and the order doesn't matter. You can merge two guest lists (union), find people registered for both workshops (intersection), identify people at workshop A but not B (difference), or pair every attendee from city X with every venue in city Y (Cartesian product).

Now introduce seating. A **relation** is the seating chart — a set of pairs (attendee, table). One attendee might sit at multiple tables (if they move around), and one table might have many attendees. The relation captures any pattern of connections without restriction.

But the hotel assigns each attendee a room key. That assignment is a **function** — each attendee gets exactly one room. If no two attendees share a room, the assignment is **injective**. If every room is occupied, it is **surjective**. If both — every attendee has a unique room and every room is occupied — it is **bijective**, a perfect one-to-one matching.

The bijection case is particularly powerful. It means you can recover the attendee from the room number just as easily as you can find the room from the attendee — the mapping is perfectly reversible. This reversibility is the mathematical core of encryption, perfect hash functions, and Cantor's theory of infinite set sizes.

sections.title: Sets: Definitions and Core Operations
sections.content:
A set A is defined by its **membership predicate** — for any object x, either x ∈ A (x is a member) or x ∉ A (it is not). Sets can be described by explicit listing: A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, or by set-builder notation: A = {x ∈ ℤ | x > 0 ∧ x < 5}. The **empty set** ∅ = {} has no members and is a subset of every set.

The six fundamental set operations you must know cold:

**Union A ∪ B** = {x | x ∈ A ∨ x ∈ B}. Elements in A or B or both. Like SQL `UNION` — all rows from either table.

**Intersection A ∩ B** = {x | x ∈ A ∧ x ∈ B}. Elements in both A and B. Like SQL `INNER JOIN` — only matching rows.

**Difference A \\ B** = {x | x ∈ A ∧ x ∉ B}. Elements in A but not B. Like SQL `EXCEPT`. Note: A \\ B ≠ B \\ A in general.

**Symmetric difference A △ B** = (A ∪ B) \\ (A ∩ B) = (A \\ B) ∪ (B \\ A). Elements in exactly one of A or B. The XOR of sets.

**Complement Aᶜ** = {x ∈ U | x ∉ A} where U is the universal set under discussion. Context-dependent.

**Cartesian product A × B** = {(a,b) | a ∈ A, b ∈ B}. All ordered pairs from the two sets. |A × B| = |A| · |B|. This is the raw material from which relations are built.

Important **identities** to internalise (they are used constantly in proofs):
- De Morgan's laws: (A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ and (A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ
- Distributivity: A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C)
- A ∪ ∅ = A, A ∩ ∅ = ∅, A ∪ A = A, A ∩ A = A (idempotence)

The **power set** P(A) is the set of all subsets of A — including ∅ and A itself. If |A| = n then |P(A)| = 2ⁿ. For A = {a, b, c}: P(A) = {∅, {a}, {b}, {c}, {a,b}, {a,c}, {b,c}, {a,b,c}} — eight elements. The exponential growth of power sets is why reasoning about all possible subsets is often computationally intractable.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: JavaScript's built-in `Set` object makes union, intersection, and difference clean one-liners via spread and `filter`. The Cartesian product is a double nested loop — its output size is |A| × |B|. The power set accumulator doubles the subsets array for each new element, producing exactly 2^n subsets. Note how `symDiff` is computed as `union \ intersection` — a neat application of De Morgan thinking.

sections.title: Relations: Structure Between Elements
sections.content:
A **binary relation** R from set A to set B is any subset of A × B. We write aRb (equivalently (a,b) ∈ R) to say 'a is related to b under R'. When A = B we say R is a relation **on** A — a relation from a set to itself.

Examples of relations on familiar sets:
- 'divides' on ℤ⁺: (2,6) ∈ R because 2 divides 6; (3,7) ∉ R.
- 'is a substring of' on strings: ('ab', 'xaby') ∈ R.
- 'is an ancestor of' on people.
- 'can reach in one step' on graph vertices — the adjacency relation.

Relations are classified by four structural **properties**. Let R be a relation on A:

**Reflexive**: ∀a ∈ A, aRa. Every element is related to itself. Example: ≤ is reflexive (1≤1); < is not (1 is not < 1).

**Symmetric**: ∀a,b ∈ A, aRb → bRa. If a is related to b, then b is related to a. Example: 'is a sibling of' is symmetric; 'is the parent of' is not.

**Antisymmetric**: ∀a,b ∈ A, aRb ∧ bRa → a = b. If two distinct elements relate to each other, they must be equal. Example: ≤ is antisymmetric (if x ≤ y and y ≤ x then x = y). Note: antisymmetric is not the same as 'not symmetric'.

**Transitive**: ∀a,b,c ∈ A, aRb ∧ bRc → aRc. Relationships chain. Example: 'is an ancestor of', '<', '⊆'.

These four properties combine to define the two most important families of relations in computer science: **equivalence relations** and **partial orders**.

sections.title: Equivalence Relations and Partitions
sections.content:
An **equivalence relation** is a relation that is simultaneously reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. The canonical example is equality itself, but equivalence relations generalise equality to 'behaves the same as' in some well-defined sense.

The fundamental theorem of equivalence relations: every equivalence relation R on a set A **partitions** A into disjoint, non-empty subsets called **equivalence classes** such that:
- Every element belongs to exactly one class.
- Two elements a, b are in the same class if and only if aRb.

The equivalence class of element a is written [a] = {b ∈ A | aRb}.

**Modular arithmetic** is the most important example. The relation 'a ≡ b (mod n)' — read 'a is congruent to b mod n', meaning n divides (a − b) — is an equivalence relation on ℤ that partitions integers into n classes [0], [1], …, [n−1] based on remainder when divided by n. This partition is the foundation of clock arithmetic, hash table bucket assignment, cyclic scheduling, and cryptographic number theory.

**String equivalence** in parsers: two strings are equivalent if they generate the same parse tree — the equivalence classes form the grammar's non-terminals.

**Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)** data structure is a direct implementation of equivalence classes. It maintains a collection of disjoint sets under two operations: `find(x)` returns the representative (canonical element) of x's equivalence class, and `union(x, y)` merges the classes of x and y. This structure underpins Kruskal's MST algorithm, network connectivity problems, and image segmentation.

The set of all equivalence classes of A under R is called the **quotient set** A/R. Its size tells you how many distinct 'kinds' of elements exist under the equivalence. For ℤ mod n: |ℤ/≡ₙ| = n.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    Z["Integers ℤ"]
    Z --> C0["Class 0\n…-6, -3, 0, 3, 6…"]
    Z --> C1["Class 1\n…-5, -2, 1, 4, 7…"]
    Z --> C2["Class 2\n…-4, -1, 2, 5, 8…"]

    C1 --> Q
    C2 --> Q
sections.caption: Modular arithmetic mod 3 partitions all integers into exactly 3 equivalence classes by remainder. The quotient set ℤ/≡₃ has 3 elements — one per class.

sections.title: Partial Orders, Total Orders, and Hasse Diagrams
sections.content:
A **partial order** is a relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive. Partial orders model hierarchies where not all pairs need to be comparable. The symbol ≤ (or ⊴, or ≼) is conventionally used for a generic partial order.

A set together with a partial order is called a **partially ordered set** or **poset**. Classic examples:
- **(P(A), ⊆)**: the power set ordered by subset inclusion. {1} and {2} are incomparable — neither is a subset of the other.
- **(ℤ⁺, |)**: positive integers ordered by divisibility. 3 and 4 are incomparable (neither divides the other); 2 | 4 so 2 ≤ 4.
- **(Tasks, 'must happen before')**: prerequisite relationships in build systems, course schedules, or dependency graphs.

A **total order** (also called a linear order) strengthens a partial order by adding **comparability**: for every pair a, b either a ≤ b or b ≤ a (or both, i.e., a = b). Real numbers, integers, and strings under lexicographic order are all totally ordered. Total orders are what sorting algorithms require.

In a poset, a **maximal element** m has no element strictly above it (nothing that m < x). A **maximum** (greatest element) is an element that is above everything else — a maximum is unique if it exists, but a poset can have many maximal elements. Similarly for **minimal** vs **minimum**.

**Topological sort** is the process of finding a linear extension of a partial order — a total order consistent with the partial order. If the poset is represented as a DAG, topological sort gives a valid sequence. The existence of a topological sort is equivalent to the DAG having no cycles.

**Hasse diagrams** visualise posets: draw a node for each element, draw an edge from a to b going upward if a ≤ b and there is no c with a ≤ c ≤ b (no intermediate element). The transitive and reflexive edges are implicit.

sections.caption: Hasse diagram for divisibility on {1,2,3,4,6,12}. An upward edge from a to b means a divides b (with no intermediate divisor). 3 and 4 are incomparable — neither divides the other.

sections.title: Functions: The Heart of Computation
sections.content:
A **function** f: A → B is a relation on A × B with the **single-value property**: for every a ∈ A there exists exactly one b ∈ B such that (a, b) ∈ f. We write f(a) = b. A is the **domain**, B is the **codomain**, and the set of all actual outputs {f(a) | a ∈ A} is the **image** (or range) of f — the image is a subset of the codomain but need not equal it.

The three key classifications:

**Injective (one-to-one)**: f(x) = f(y) ⟹ x = y. No two distinct inputs produce the same output. Equivalently, distinct inputs always produce distinct outputs. The image has the same size as the domain. For finite sets, injective requires |A| ≤ |B|.

**Surjective (onto)**: ∀ b ∈ B, ∃ a ∈ A such that f(a) = b. Every element of the codomain is the image of at least one input. The image equals the entire codomain. For finite sets, surjective requires |A| ≥ |B|.

**Bijective**: both injective and surjective. There is a perfect one-to-one correspondence between domain and codomain. For finite sets, bijective requires |A| = |B|. A bijection is always **invertible**: the inverse function f⁻¹: B → A is well-defined and also bijective.

Bijections are far more than a curiosity — they are a fundamental tool:
- **Counting**: to show two finite sets have the same size, exhibit a bijection. This is the only way to define 'same size' for infinite sets.
- **Cryptography**: a cipher is a family of bijections on the message space. The key selects which bijection to apply; decryption applies the inverse.
- **Perfect hashing**: a perfect hash function is an injection from keys to table indices — no two keys collide.
- **Type isomorphisms**: in type theory, two types are isomorphic if there is a bijection between their values. `Either () ()` and `Bool` are isomorphic — both have exactly two values.

**Composition**: if f: A → B and g: B → C then (g ∘ f): A → C is defined by (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)). Read right-to-left: apply f first, then g. Composition is **associative**: (h ∘ g) ∘ f = h ∘ (g ∘ f). It is not generally commutative: g ∘ f ≠ f ∘ g.

Composition preserves structure: the composition of two injections is injective; the composition of two surjections is surjective; the composition of two bijections is bijective.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    FN["f: A → B"] --> INJ["Injective
f(x)=f(y) implies x=y
no output is shared"]
    FN --> SUR["Surjective
for all b exists a: f(a)=b
every output is hit"]
    INJ --> BIJ["Bijective = Injective + Surjective
perfect 1-to-1 correspondence"]
    SUR --> BIJ
    BIJ --> INV["Invertible: f-inverse exists
and is also bijective"]
sections.caption: A bijection is the intersection of injective and surjective. Only bijections have inverses. For finite sets: injective implies |A| ≤ |B|, surjective implies |A| ≥ |B|, bijective implies |A| = |B|.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The `isInjective` check is O(n) using a Set for O(1) lookups — it detects the first duplicate output immediately. The `isSurjective` check builds the image set and verifies every codomain element appears. The `compose` utility applies functions right-to-left using `reduceRight`, matching mathematical notation exactly. The final example confirms that composing two bijections yields another bijection.

sections.title: Equivalence Relations in Code: Union-Find
sections.content:
**Union-Find** (also called Disjoint Set Union, DSU) is the canonical algorithmic instantiation of equivalence relations. It solves the dynamic connectivity problem: given a universe of n elements, support two operations — `union(x, y)` (merge the equivalence classes of x and y) and `find(x)` (return the representative of x's class) — in near-constant amortised time.

The data structure maintains a forest of trees. Each tree represents one equivalence class; the root is the canonical representative. Two optimisations together achieve the near-O(1) bound:

**Path compression**: on a `find` call, flatten the path from node to root so every node on the path points directly to the root. Future finds from those nodes are O(1).

**Union by rank** (or union by size): always attach the smaller tree under the root of the larger tree, keeping trees shallow.

With both optimisations, the amortised cost per operation is O(α(n)) where α is the inverse Ackermann function — for all practical n, α(n) ≤ 4. Effectively constant.

Real-world applications: Kruskal's minimum spanning tree (merge components as edges are added), network connectivity queries, image segmentation (which pixels are in the same connected component?), detecting cycles in undirected graphs, and offline LCA (lowest common ancestor) queries.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Path compression in `find` makes the tree maximally flat on access — a future find from any node on the path is O(1). Union by rank keeps the tree height logarithmically bounded, but path compression in practice makes it even flatter. The cycle detection example directly mirrors the mathematical definition: an edge creates a cycle if and only if both endpoints are already in the same equivalence class (connected component).

sections.title: Bijections and Cantor: Counting the Uncountable
sections.content:
Bijections are the tool Cantor used in the 1870s to build a rigorous theory of **infinite set sizes** (cardinalities). Two sets have the same cardinality if there exists a bijection between them — even for infinite sets.

**Countably infinite sets**: A set is countably infinite if there is a bijection between it and the natural numbers ℕ = {0, 1, 2, 3, …}. Surprising facts:
- The integers ℤ are countably infinite (bijection: 0↔0, 1↔1, -1↔2, 2↔3, -2↔4, …).
- The rationals ℚ are countably infinite — Cantor's diagonal enumeration provides a bijection from ℕ to ℚ.
- The union of countably many countable sets is countable.

**Uncountably infinite sets**: Cantor's diagonal argument proves there is no bijection from ℕ to the real numbers ℝ. Assume such a bijection f exists. Construct a real number r whose n-th decimal digit differs from the n-th decimal digit of f(n). This r cannot equal f(n) for any n — contradicting surjectivity. Therefore, ℝ is **strictly larger** than ℕ. We say |ℕ| = ℵ₀ (aleph-null) and |ℝ| = 2^ℵ₀ = ℵ₁ (under the continuum hypothesis).

Why does this matter for CS? The set of all computer programs is countably infinite (programs are finite strings over a finite alphabet, and all such strings can be enumerated). The set of all mathematical functions from ℕ to ℕ is uncountably infinite. Therefore there exist mathematical functions that **no computer program can compute** — a pure counting argument. This is the seed of computability theory: most functions are uncomputable, not because we haven't found the algorithm yet, but because no algorithm can exist.

**Historical context:** Georg Cantor published his diagonal argument in 1891, building on earlier work from 1874. It was deeply controversial — Cantor was attacked by prominent mathematicians of his era, including Kronecker ('God made the integers; all else is the work of man'). Today Cantor's set theory is the foundation of modern mathematics. The same diagonal argument pattern appears in Godel's incompleteness theorems (1931), Turing's proof that the Halting Problem is undecidable (1936), and Russell's paradox — one of the most powerful proof techniques in all of mathematics.

sections.title: Relations in Databases: The Relational Model
sections.content:
The relational database model — invented by E.F. Codd at IBM in 1970 and still the dominant paradigm today — is literally built on the mathematical concept of relations. A database **table** is a relation: a set of tuples (rows) where each tuple is an element of the Cartesian product of the attribute domains.

A `Users` table with columns (id: ℤ, name: String, age: ℤ) is a subset of ℤ × String × ℤ — a ternary relation. The **primary key** constraint ensures the id column defines an **injective** function from rows to integers: no two rows share an id. A **foreign key** constraint establishes a relation between two tables and requires referential integrity — every value in the foreign key column must appear in the referenced table's primary key column.

**SQL operations map directly to set operations:**
- `UNION` → A ∪ B (with `UNION ALL` removing the implicit deduplication)
- `INTERSECT` → A ∩ B
- `EXCEPT` / `MINUS` → A \\ B
- `JOIN` → a computed Cartesian product with a selection condition
- `CROSS JOIN` → the full Cartesian product A × B

**Relational algebra** — the formal query language underlying SQL — uses six primitive operations: select (σ), project (π), Cartesian product (×), union (∪), difference (\\), and rename (ρ). Every SQL query can be expressed as a composition of these six operations. SQL's `WHERE` clause is σ (selection), `SELECT column_list` is π (projection).

**Common misconceptions and interview traps:**

**'Antisymmetric means not symmetric'** — Wrong. A relation can be both symmetric and antisymmetric. The only relation on A that satisfies both is the identity relation {(a,a) | a ∈ A} — symmetric because aRb → bRa trivially (since only aRa exists), antisymmetric because aRb ∧ bRa → a = b (which holds vacuously for distinct pairs).

**'The codomain equals the image'** — Not in general. f: ℝ → ℝ defined by f(x) = x² has codomain ℝ but image [0, ∞). The function is not surjective. Interview questions often test whether you distinguish codomain from image.

**'A bijection requires |A| = |B|'** — This is true for finite sets, but not the definition. For infinite sets, the definition is: a bijection exists. Cantor showed |ℕ| = |ℚ| (equal cardinality via bijection) even though intuitively rationals seem 'more'.

**'Equivalence relations and equality are the same thing'** — Equality is one equivalence relation, but any reflexive, symmetric, transitive relation qualifies. Equivalence classes can be coarse (all integers mod 2 = two classes) or fine (equality on ℤ = infinitely many singleton classes).

**Topological sort exists iff** the relation (DAG) has no cycles — cycles would require a ≤ b ≤ a for distinct a, b, violating antisymmetry.

items: **Sets** are unordered collections of distinct elements. The six core operations — union (∪), intersection (∩), difference (\\), symmetric difference (△), complement, and Cartesian product (×) — map directly to SQL operations, type system combinators, and set-theoretic proofs. The power set P(A) has 2^|A| elements, an exponential that makes exhaustive search intractable.

A **relation** on A × B is any subset of ordered pairs. Four properties — reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive — classify relations into families. An **equivalence relation** (reflexive + symmetric + transitive) partitions its set into disjoint equivalence classes; modular arithmetic and Union-Find are canonical CS implementations.

A **partial order** (reflexive + antisymmetric + transitive) models hierarchies where some pairs are incomparable. A **total order** adds comparability (every pair is related) — what sorting algorithms require. Topological sort finds a linear extension of a partial order and exists if and only if the underlying directed graph has no cycles.

A **function** f: A → B is injective (one-to-one) if distinct inputs give distinct outputs, surjective (onto) if every codomain element is reachable, and **bijective** if both. Bijections are invertible and imply |A| = |B| for finite sets. They are the mathematical core of encryption, perfect hashing, and counting arguments.

**Function composition** (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)) applies f first, then g. Composition is associative but not commutative. Injections compose to injections; surjections to surjections; bijections to bijections — these closure properties are used constantly in type theory and algebra.

**Cantor's diagonal argument** proves there is no bijection from ℕ to ℝ — the reals are strictly larger than the naturals. Since programs are countable but mathematical functions are not, most functions are uncomputable. This is the foundation of computability theory.

The **relational database model** is literally built on mathematical relations: tables are subsets of Cartesian products of attribute domains; SQL's UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT directly implement set operations; relational algebra's six primitives can express every SQL query.

quiz.question: Which set operation produces exactly the elements that are in A or B but NOT in both?
quiz.explanation: Symmetric difference A △ B = (A ∪ B) \ (A ∩ B) contains elements in exactly one of the two sets. Union (A ∪ B) includes elements in either or both. Intersection (A ∩ B) keeps only elements in both. Difference (A \ B) keeps elements in A but not B — but misses elements in B but not A.

quiz.question: If |A| = 4, how many elements does the power set P(A) contain?
quiz.explanation: |P(A)| = 2^|A| = 2⁴ = 16. The power set includes all subsets: the empty set, all 4 singletons, all 6 two-element subsets, all 4 three-element subsets, and A itself. 1 + 4 + 6 + 4 + 1 = 16. This exponential growth is why exhaustive subset search is intractable for large sets.

quiz.question: An equivalence relation must satisfy which three properties?
quiz.explanation: An equivalence relation is reflexive (aRa for all a), symmetric (aRb implies bRa), and transitive (aRb and bRc implies aRc). These three properties guarantee the relation partitions the set into disjoint equivalence classes. Reflexive + antisymmetric + transitive defines a partial order, not an equivalence relation.

quiz.question: Function f: {1,2,3} → {a,b,c,d} with f(1)=a, f(2)=b, f(3)=c. What are its properties?
quiz.explanation: f is injective: distinct inputs (1,2,3) map to distinct outputs (a,b,c), so f(x)=f(y) implies x=y. f is NOT surjective: element d in the codomain {a,b,c,d} is never the output of any input. For surjectivity, every codomain element must be reachable. A bijection would require |domain| = |codomain|, but here 3 < 4.

quiz.question: What is the Cartesian product A × B if A = {1,2} and B = {x,y}?
quiz.explanation: A × B = {(a,b) | a ∈ A, b ∈ B} — every element of A paired with every element of B. With A={1,2} and B={x,y}: {(1,x),(1,y),(2,x),(2,y)}. Size = |A| × |B| = 2 × 2 = 4. Option A only has 2 pairs (a partial matching). Option C has the pairs reversed (that would be B × A). Option D is just the union, not ordered pairs.

quiz.question: A partial order differs from a total order because in a partial order:
options: Some pairs of elements may be incomparable (neither a≤b nor b≤a)
Every element must relate to itself via symmetry
quiz.explanation: In a partial order, pairs of elements can be incomparable — neither aRb nor bRa. For example, under subset inclusion: {1} and {2} are incomparable (neither is a subset of the other). A total order adds the comparability axiom: for every pair (a,b), either a≤b or b≤a. Total orders are what sorting algorithms need. Transitivity is required for both.

quiz.question: If f: A → B is bijective, which statement is always true?
options: The inverse f⁻¹: B → A exists and is also bijective
f must map every element to itself
quiz.explanation: A bijection is invertible by definition: since f is injective, no two inputs share an output, so we can unambiguously reverse each mapping; since f is surjective, every b has a preimage. The inverse f⁻¹: B → A maps each b to its unique preimage, and is itself bijective. For finite sets, bijective implies |A| = |B| (not greater). The function need not be the identity.

quiz.question: Why does Cantor's diagonal argument imply that most mathematical functions are uncomputable?
options: Computers can only handle finite inputs
The set of programs is countable but the set of all functions from ℕ to ℕ is uncountable
Diagonal arguments only apply to real numbers, not programs
Computability requires a bijection between inputs and outputs
quiz.explanation: Programs are finite strings over a finite alphabet, so the set of all programs is countably infinite (same cardinality as ℕ). The set of all functions from ℕ to ℕ is uncountably infinite (|ℕ^ℕ| = 2^ℵ₀ > ℵ₀). Since there is no bijection between a countable and an uncountable set, most functions cannot be the input-output behaviour of any program — they are uncomputable, not just undiscovered.

quiz.question: In the Union-Find data structure, path compression on a find(x) call does what?
options: Splits the equivalence class of x into smaller classes
Makes every node on the path from x to the root point directly to the root
Swaps x with its parent to maintain sorted order
Deletes x from the data structure
quiz.explanation: Path compression flattens the tree: when find(x) traverses from x to the root, it makes every visited node point directly to the root. Future find calls from those nodes become O(1). Combined with union by rank, this achieves amortised O(α(n)) per operation where α is the inverse Ackermann function — effectively constant for all practical n.

quiz.question: Function composition (g ∘ f)(x) is defined as:
options: f(g(x)): apply g first, then f
g(f(x)): apply f first, then g
g(x) × f(x): multiply the two outputs
g(x) + f(x): add the two outputs
quiz.explanation: (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)): f is applied first to x, then g is applied to the result. The notation reads right-to-left — the rightmost function in a composition chain is applied first. Composition is associative — (h ∘ g) ∘ f = h ∘ (g ∘ f) — but not generally commutative: g ∘ f ≠ f ∘ g. If both f and g are bijections, their composition is also a bijection.
